requirements.requirement: On node1, restrict cron scheduling so that only root and opsadmin can use crontab
requirements.summary: Baseline showed no /etc/cron.allow or /etc/cron.deny (open access to all users, evidenced by cmd-09f3c60c68ad446f and cmd-9849ce43aae242ca). Executor created /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' with mode 644 owned root:root (cmd-0389ec4129574c1e), and this file was confirmed present with the same content after a full node restart (cmd-ff4d6a85e15048ea), demonstrating both the change and its persistence.

requirements.requirement: The restriction must be effectively enforced (non-listed users denied, listed users/root allowed)
requirements.summary: Before applying the allow-list, both testuser1 and opsadmin could install crontabs (exit 0, cmd-5068770dff034c3c). After applying /etc/cron.allow, testuser1's crontab install failed with 'not allowed to use this program' (exit 1) while opsadmin and root succeeded (exit 0), directly demonstrating enforcement (cmd-2747748dab2c44cf). Post-restart, opsadmin was again shown able to schedule and remove a cron job (cmd-ff4d6a85e15048ea), confirming the control remains functional after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Do not leave unnecessary test artifacts (temporary verification user/crontabs) behind
requirements.summary: The temporary testuser1 account and its crontab, along with the test crontabs used for opsadmin/root during verification, were removed (cmd-86a175e976044c8a); the final post-restart check confirms testuser1 no longer exists and no stray crontabs remain outside the intentional final opsadmin test which was itself removed (cmd-ff4d6a85e15048ea).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline/boot identity, restart acknowledgement, differing post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id fa1e87e6-00f3-42d2-acc5-ad1df6c3d16a and healthy cron.service/cron.allow state were captured (cmd-eee6bd2b86bc48fb, consistent with global:before_prepare:node1:boot-identity). A background reboot returned an acknowledgement before disconnect (cmd-99779976f07e4966), SSH was refused during the reboot window (cmd-eb69671bf6d44256), and the node became reachable again with a new boot_id 4fd739f1-1bc9-41de-bc63-c54f8e7dc885 (cmd-2f1f3a93cbe5478c), matching the fixed global:after_executor:node1:boot-identity snapshot. Post-restart state shows cron.service active, /etc/cron.allow intact, and opsadmin's cron access functional (cmd-ff4d6a85e15048ea).

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin via /etc/cron.allow, demonstrated enforcement with a clear before/after denial test on a throwaway user, cleaned up all test artifacts, and completed the mandatory restart protocol with direct evidence of a changed boot identity and full post-restart recovery of the cron configuration and its enforcement. All material outcomes are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence and no unaddressed hygiene concerns.
limitations: Post-restart verification of the restriction relies only on confirming opsadmin's continued access and file persistence; a repeat denial test against a non-listed user after reboot was not performed, though this is a minor gap given the file was shown byte-identical and cron.service was active.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace to a clear purpose: creating opsadmin (needed to satisfy the task's allow-list), creating a temporary testuser1 for negative-case verification (bounded and fully removed via cmd-86a175e976044c8a), writing /etc/cron.allow (the core task change), test crontab installs for both baseline and post-fix verification (each removed immediately after use, e.g. cmd-86a175e976044c8a and within cmd-ff4d6a85e15048ea), and a single deliberate reboot for the mandated restart protocol. No unnecessary, broad, destructive, or unreverted mutations were found; the lifecycle diff shows only the expected boot-id change and ephemeral systemd timesync temp directories, no residue attributable to executor actions beyond the intended /etc/cron.allow and opsadmin account.
